chunks: Why chip ground potential varies. The question: Why would the ground potential of a chip vary?
Ground is supposed to be a perfect 0 volts reference. But ground on a chip is real metal, with some resistance and some inductance.
Whenever current flows through it, and especially when the current changes fast, a voltage appears. So the chip's internal ground can sit above or below the board's ground.
The biggest cause in digital chips is many outputs switching at once, which is called ground bounce.
Think of the floor of a building as your zero height.
If a large crowd stomps at the same moment, the floor flexes, and everything resting on it seems to jump relative to the world outside. Ground bounce is the same.
The more people stomp, and the faster they do it, the bigger the bounce. When the floor moves, every reading taken from it is off.
Output load current flows through the die ground, then through the package/board ground impedance (R g, L g) to the board ground.
The voltage across that impedance is the ground bounce. It is largest when the current changes fastest.
Ground: the reference point that everything else is measured against, called 0 volts. Inductance: how strongly a connection resists fast changes in current.
Ground bounce: the die's ground voltage jumping because of current changes through the package.
Simultaneous switching: many outputs changing at the same moment, so their currents add.
Decoupling capacitor: a small capacitor next to the chip that supplies quick bursts of current locally.
Say four outputs each charge a small load (10 picofarads, a tiny capacitance) to 3. 3 volts, and each switch takes 2 nanoseconds.
Together they change the ground current by about 0. 13 amps every nanosecond. The package ground path has 1 nanohenries of inductance.
The voltage across an inductor is its inductance times how fast the current changes: 1 nanohenries times 0. 13 amps/ns about 0. 13 volts, or 130 millivolts.
That can make a quiet pin glitch. Double the outputs and the bounce doubles. Halve the switching time and it roughly quadruples. That is the whole idea.
"Ground isn't ideal. It has resistance and inductance, so current through it makes voltage.
The big one is ground bounce: when many outputs switch, their current changes fast through bond wire and pin inductance, and L di over dt lifts the die's ground above board ground.
Add IR drop in the grid and planes, shared return paths, substrate coupling and ground loops.
Fix with more ground pins, decoupling at the die, slower edges, and low-inductance packages."
